title: Rav Eina
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: He was among the elders of Pumbedita in the time of Rav Yehuda, as in Sanhedrin 17b: the elders of Pumbedita were Rav Yehuda and Rav Eina; and there, 26b, he disagrees with Rav Yehuda.

It is possible that he is the one called Rav Eina Saba, as in Pesachim 88a and Megillah 14b, where he challenged Rav Nachman, who replied to him: "Eina Saba" — and some say, "the black (or: dark) pitcher" — "from me and you the teaching will be concluded."
He is also mentioned in a halakhic discussion in Rosh Hashanah 26a, objecting against the words of R' Shmuel bar Yitzchak.
And in Sukkah 48b: "What is the source of this?" Rav Eina said: for Scripture says, etc.
And in Bava Kamma 19b he asked: what is the law of an animal wagging its tail?

And in Chullin 84b we find that Rav Eina taught at the entrance of the Exilarch's house that one who slaughters for a sick person on the Sabbath is obligated to cover [the blood]. Rabbah said to them: "He is saying something astonishing (a surprising statement); remove his public interpreter from him," and Hyman reports that Rashi explains: they should cut out his tongue. Hyman argues: Without doubt, our teacher's intent is that his language needs correcting, since he did not express himself well regarding the halakha in what he said. But it is very difficult to say that Rabbah would say this about Rav Eina, who was already an old man in the time of Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman. Hyman considers the reading he finds in Dikdukei Soferim more correct, with Ravina as the speaker. If so, he argues, this is not the earlier Rav Eina but Rav Eina of the Saboraic sages, who ruled in Sura, as is cited in the Epistle of Rav Sherira Gaon, part 2, chapter 4, whose words are: Rav Eina in Sura, and Rabbi Simuniya in Pumbedita, and after that Rav Rabbai of Mirov (also mentioned elsewhere in the Gemara). Hyman identifies Ravina as Ravina bar Umtzia, who died in the year written התי״ז of the Seleucid era.

notes.text: The named Davidson Megillah14b makes Rav Nachman reply to Rav Eina, using Eina Saba or dark vessel. Chullin84b has public interpreter, while Hyman reports Rashi’s tongue explanation and offers his own softened reading.
Hyman distinguishes earlier and later Eina and reports a Ravina reading. The supplied year התי״ז is retained literally; its precise numeral and therefore its date remain unresolved.

The saved William Davidson Megillah 14b paragraphs explicitly have Rav Eina Saba challenging Rav Nachman, followed by the reply to Eina Saba; the saved Chullin 84b paragraph has Rabbah and the interpreter phrase. Hyman’s “it is possible,” “without doubt,” preference for the Ravina reading, interpretation of Rashi, later-Eina identification, chronology, and epistle quotation retain their stated force as his claims. Rashi, Dikdukei Soferim, and the epistle have not been freshly collated here; the supplied התי״ז is retained without a numeral or era conversion. The abbreviated title in R' Shmuel bar Yitzchak remains literal. The p007 source hold is retained; no person, teacher relationship, or date is independently established by these paragraphs.

The consulted Sanhedrin 17b lists Rav Eina with Rav Yehuda among the elders of Pumbedita. In both Pesachim 88a and Megillah 14b, Rav Eina Saba challenges Rav Nachman, who replies with the alternative forms of address. Chullin 84b names Rabbah, and the Vilna Rashi gives both a literal tongue-cutting gloss and an alternate reading in which the interpreter is removed from before him to shame him. Hyman’s explanation about correcting the language and his preference for a Ravina reading remain his own conclusions. The Oxford 1888 text of the Epistle (1:111) names Ravina from Amtzia in Adar in the context of its תתי״ז chronology, followed later in the paragraph by Eina in Sura, Simona in Pumbedita and Rabbai of Rov. The supplied date התי״ז is retained without conversion. The Epistle passage and the earlier Talmudic appearances do not by themselves identify which Rav Eina is meant in Chullin.
